readings.c1s1:
¶
'''uncontemned''' (un-kon-temd′), ''a.'' Not despised; not contemned. ''Shak.'', Hen. VIII., iii. 2. 10.

'''uncontended''' (un-kon-ten′ded), ''a.'' Not disputed for; not contested. ''Dryden'', Æneid, v.

'''uncontented†''' (un-kọn-ten′ted), ''a.'' Discontented. ''Daniel'', Philotas, Ded.

'''uncontentedness†''' (un-kọn-ten′ted-nes), ''n.'' Discontentedness. ''Hammond'', Works, I. 478.

'''uncontentingness†''' (un-kọn-ten′ting-nes), ''n.'' Want of power to satisfy. ''Boyle'', Works, I. 261.

'''uncontestable†''' (un-kọn-tes′tạ-bl), ''a.'' Incontestable. ''Locke.''

'''uncontested''' (un-kọn-tes′ted), ''a.'' Not contested; not disputed; hence, evident; indisputable. ''Sir R. Blackmore'', Creation.

'''uncontradictable''' (un-kon-tra-dik′ta-bl), ''a.'' That cannot be contradicted. ''Carlyle.''

'''uncontradicted''' (un-kon-trạ-dik′ted), ''a.'' Not contradicted; not denied: as, ''uncontradicted'' testimony. ''Bp. Pearson'', Expos. of Creed, xi.

'''uncontriving''' (un-kọn-trī′ving), ''a.'' Not contriving; deficient in contrivance. [Rare.]
{{smaller block|The savage, ''uncontriving'' man.
{{right|''Goldsmith'', Animated Nature. (''Latham.'')}}}}

'''uncontrollable''' (un-kọn-trō′lạ-bl), ''a.'' '''1.''' That cannot be controlled or ruled; ungovernable; intolerant of restraint: as, an ''uncontrollable'' temper; ''uncontrollable'' subjects; ''uncontrollable'' events.—'''2†.''' Indisputable; irrefragable. [Rare.]
readings.c1s4:
¶
'''unconversant''' (un-kon′vėr-sa̤nt), ''a.'' Not conversant; not familiarly acquainted: followed usually by ''with'' before an object, sometimes by ''in.''
{{smaller block|''Unconversant in'' disquisitions of this kind.
{{right|''Madox'', Exchequer, Pref.}}}}
readings.c2s1:
¶
'''unconversion''' (un-kọn-vėr′shọn), ''n.'' The state of being unconverted; impenitence. [Rare.]

'''unconverted''' (un-kọn-vėr′ted), ''a.'' Not converted; not changed in opinion; specifically, not brought to accept a (specified) religious faith; in ''theol.'', not having abandoned a sinful life: as, the ''unconverted.''
{{smaller block|''Unconverted'' to Christianity.
{{right|''Jer. Taylor'', Of Repentance, viii.}}}}

'''unconvertible''' (un-kọn-vėr′ti-bl), ''a.'' Not convertible; that cannot be changed from one thing or form to another: as, lead is ''unconvertible'' into silver.
{{smaller block|''Unconvertible'' ignorance. ''Congreve'', Love for Love, iv. 12.}}

'''uncord''' (un-kôrd′), ''v. t.'' [< ''un-''<sup>2</sup> + ''cord''<sup>1</sup>.] To loose from cords; unfasten or unbind: as, to ''uncord'' a bed; to ''uncord'' a package.

'''uncork''' (un-kôrk′), ''v. t.'' [< ''un-''<sup>2</sup> + ''cork''<sup>1</sup>.] '''1.''' To draw the cork from; open by drawing the cork, as a bottle.—'''2.''' To allow to flow out, as if by removing a cork, as words, feelings, and the like; cause (a person) to speak. [Colloq. or slang.]

'''uncorrect†''' (un-kọ-rekt′), ''a.'' Incorrect. ''Dryden'', Wild Gallant, Pref.
readings.c2s2:
¶
'''uncorrespondency†''' (un-kor-e-spon′den-si), ''n.'' The state of being uncorrespondent, or not mutually adapted or agreeable. ''Bp. Gauden.''

'''uncorrespondent†''' (un-kor-e-spon′dent), ''a.'' Not correspondent; not suitable, adapted, or agreeable. ''Bp. Gauden.''

'''uncorrigible†''' (un-kor′i-ji-bl), ''a.'' [< ME. ''uncorrigible''; < ''un-''<sup>1</sup> + ''corrigible''.] Incorrigible. ''Wyclif.''

'''uncorrupt''' (un-ko̤-rupt′), ''a.'' Not corrupt; not depraved; not perverted; incorrupt; pure: as, an ''uncorrupt'' judgment; an ''uncorrupt'' text.

{{smaller block|For the rest, my Lord Clifford was a valiant ''uncorrupt'' gentleman.
{{right|''Evelyn'', Diary, Aug. 18, 1673.}}}}

'''uncorrupted''' (un-ko̤-rup′ted), ''a.'' Not corrupted, in any sense; not debased; not vitiated; not depraved; not decomposed.

{{smaller block|In the chapel belonging to it lies the body of St. Susorius their founder, as yet ''uncorrupted'' though dead many hundreds of yeares.
{{right|''Evelyn'', Diary, Oct. 25, 1644.}}}}

'''uncorruptedness''' (un-ko̤-rup′ted-nes), ''n.'' The state of being uncorrupted. ''Milton'', Areopagitica.

'''uncorruptibility†''' (un-ko̤-rup-ti-bil′i̤-ti), ''n.'' [< ME. ''uncorruptibilitie''; < ''uncorruptible'' + ''-ity'' (see ''-bility'').] Incapability of being corrupted; incorruption.

{{smaller block|In ''vncoruptibilite'' of quyete or pesible and mylde spirit.
{{right|''Wyclif'', 1 Pet. iii. 4.}}}}

'''uncorruptible†''' (un-ko̤-rup′ti-bl), ''a.'' [< ME. ''uncorruptible''; < ''un-''<sup>1</sup> + ''corruptible''.] Incorruptible. Rom. i. 23.

¶
'''uncorruption†''' (un-ko̤-rup′shọn), ''n.'' [< ME. ''uncorrupcioun''; < ''un-''<sup>1</sup> + ''corruption.''] Incorruption.
{{smaller block|Glorie and honour and ''vncoripcioun'' to hem that seken eurlastynge lyf.
{{right|''Wyclif'', Rom. ii. 7.}}}}

'''uncorruptive†''' (un-ko̤-rup′tiv), ''a.'' Incorruptible.
{{smaller block|Those other climes of ''uncorruptive'' joy.
{{right|''Glover'', Leonidas, vii. 413.}}}}

'''uncorruptly''' (un-ko̤-rupt′li), ''adv.'' In an uncorrupt manner; truly; genuinely.
{{smaller block|I shall declare ''uncorruptlye'' the sayings.
{{right|''Brende'', tr. of Quintus Curtius, fol. 198.}}}}

'''uncorruptness''' (un-ko̤-rupt′nes), ''n.'' Integrity; uprightness. Tit. ii. 7.

'''uncorven†''', ''a.'' [ME., < ''un-''<sup>1</sup> + ''corven'', pp. of ''kerven'', carve: see ''carve.''] Uncut; untrimmed.
{{smaller block|''Uncorven'' and ungrobbed lay the vyne.
{{right|''Chaucer'', Former Age, l. 14.}}}}

'''uncostly''' (un-kôst′li), ''a.'' Not costly; not of a high price or value.
{{smaller block|A man’s spirit is naturally careless of baser and ''uncostly'' materials.
{{right|''Jer. Taylor'', Works (ed. 1835), I. 841.}}}}

'''uncounselable, uncounsellable''' (un-koun′sel-a̤-bl), ''a.'' Not to be advised; not consistent with good advice or prudence. ''Clarendon'', Civil Wars.

'''uncounseled, uncounselled''' (un-koun′seld), ''a.'' [< ME. ''uncounceiled''; < ''un-''<sup>1</sup> + ''counseled.''] '''1.''' Not having counsel or advice. ''Burke'', Letter

'''uncontentedness†''' (un-kọn-ten′ted-nes), ''n.'' Discontentedness. ''Hammond'', Works, I. 478.

'''uncontentingness†''' (un-kọn-ten′ting-nes), ''n.'' Want of power to satisfy. ''Boyle'', Works, I. 261.

'''uncontested''' (un-kọn-tes′ted), ''a.'' Not contested; not disputed; hence, evident; indisputable. ''Sir R. Blackmore'', Creation.

'''uncontradictable''' (un-kon-tra-dik′ta-bl), ''a.'' That cannot be contradicted. ''Carlyle.''

'''uncontradicted''' (un-kon-trạ-dik′ted), ''a.'' Not contradicted; not denied: as, ''uncontradicted'' testimony. ''Bp. Pearson'', Expos. of Creed, xi.

'''uncontriving''' (un-kọn-trī′ving), ''a.'' Not contriving; deficient in contrivance. [Rare.]
{{smaller block|The savage, ''uncontriving'' man.
{{right|''Goldsmith'', Animated Nature. (''Latham.'')}}}}

'''uncontrollable''' (un-kọn-trō′lạ-bl), ''a.'' '''1.''' That cannot be controlled or ruled; ungovernable; intolerant of restraint: as, an ''uncontrollable'' temper; ''uncontrollable'' subjects; ''uncontrollable'' events.—'''2†.''' Indisputable; irrefragable. [Rare.]

{{smaller block|This pension was granted by reason of the King of England’s ''uncontroulable'' title to England. {{right|''Sir J. Hayward.''}}}}

'''uncontrollableness''' (un-kọn-trō′lạ-bl-nes), ''n.'' The character of being uncontrollable. ''Bp. Hall.''

'''uncontrollably''' (un-kọn-trō′lạ-bli), ''adv.'' '''1.''' In an uncontrollable manner; without being subject to control.
{{smaller block|God may ''uncontrollably'' and lawfully deal with his creatures as he pleases. {{right|''A. Tucker.''}}}}
'''2†.''' Indisputably; incontrovertibly.
{{smaller block|Abundantly and ''uncontrolably'' convincing the reality of our Saviour’s death. {{right|''Bp. Hall'', Contemplations, Christ Crucified.}}}}

'''uncontrolled''' (un-kọn-trōld′), ''a.'' '''1.''' Not controlled or governed; free.
{{smaller block|<poem>But Jove’s high will is ever ''uncontrol’d'',
The strong he withers, and confounds the bold.</poem>
{{right|''Pope'', Iliad, xvii. 197.}}}}
'''2.''' Not yielding to restraint; uncontrollable.
{{smaller block|<poem>Do I not know the ''uncontrolled'' thoughts
That youth brings with him when his blood is high?</poem>
{{right|''Beau. and Fl.'', Maid’s Tragedy, iii.}}}}
'''3†.''' Not disproved; not refuted.
{{smaller block|That Julius Cæsar was so born is an ''uncontrouled'' report. {{right|''Sir J. Hayward.''}}}}

'''uncontrolledly''' (un-kọn-trō′led-li), ''adv.'' Without control or restraint; without effectual opposition.

'''uncontroversory†''' (un-kon-trọ̄-vėr′sọ̄-ri), ''a.'' [< ''un-''<sup>1</sup> + *''controversory'', equiv. to ''controversorious''.] Free from controversy. [Rare.]
{{smaller block|An ''uncontroversory'' piety.
{{right|''Bp. Hall'', Def. of Humb. Remonst., § 2.}}}}

'''uncontroverted''' (un-kon′trọ̄-vėr-ted), ''a.'' Not controverted or disputed; not liable to be called in question.
{{smaller block|The ''uncontroverted'' certainty of mathematical science.
{{right|''Glanville.''}}}}

'''unconventional''' (un-kọn-ven′shọn-al), ''a.'' Not conventional; not bound by unswerving rules; free in character, action, or treatment.

'''unconventionality''' (un-kọn-ven-shọn-al′ị-ti), ''n.''; pl. ''unconventionalities'' (-tiz). The character or state of being unconventional; originality; freedom from rules and precedents; also, that which is unconventional; an unconventional act.
{{smaller block|Whately often offended people by the extreme ''unconventionality'' of his manners. {{right|''Encyc. Brit.'', XXIV. 530.}}

A quaint little story, notable among other ''unconventionalities'' for being a romance without even a vestige of a love story. {{right|''The Academy'', No. 877, p. 1 of adv’ts.}}}}

'''unconversable''' (un-kọn-vėr′sa-bl), ''a.'' Not free in conversation; repelling conversation; not social; reserved.
{{smaller block|I soon grew domestic with lord Halifax, and was as often with lord Somers as the formality of his nature (the only ''unconversable'' fault he had) made it agreeable to me.
{{right|''Swift'', Change in Queen’s Ministry.}}}}

'''unconversant''' (un-kon′vėr-sa̤nt), ''a.'' Not conversant; not familiarly acquainted: followed usually by ''with'' before an object, sometimes by ''in.''
{{smaller block|''Unconversant in'' disquisitions of this kind.
{{right|''Madox'', Exchequer, Pref.}}}}

'''unconversion''' (un-kọn-vėr′shọn), ''n.'' The state of being unconverted; impenitence. [Rare.]

'''unconverted''' (un-kọn-vėr′ted), ''a.'' Not converted; not changed in opinion; specifically, not brought to accept a (specified) religious faith; in ''theol.'', not having abandoned a sinful life: as, the ''unconverted.''
{{smaller block|''Unconverted'' to Christianity.
{{right|''Jer. Taylor'', Of Repentance, viii.}}}}

'''unconvertible''' (un-kọn-vėr′ti-bl), ''a.'' Not convertible; that cannot be changed from one thing or form to another: as, lead is ''unconvertible'' into silver.
{{smaller block|''Unconvertible'' ignorance. ''Congreve'', Love for Love, iv. 12.}}

'''uncord''' (un-kôrd′), ''v. t.'' [< ''un-''<sup>2</sup> + ''cord''<sup>1</sup>.] To loose from cords; unfasten or unbind: as, to ''uncord'' a bed; to ''uncord'' a package.

'''uncork''' (un-kôrk′), ''v. t.'' [< ''un-''<sup>2</sup> + ''cork''<sup>1</sup>.] '''1.''' To draw the cork from; open by drawing the cork, as a bottle.—'''2.''' To allow to flow out, as if by removing a cork, as words, feelings, and the like; cause (a person) to speak. [Colloq. or slang.]

'''uncorrect†''' (un-kọ-rekt′), ''a.'' Incorrect. ''Dryden'', Wild Gallant, Pref.

'''uncorrespondency†''' (un-kor-e-spon′den-si), ''n.'' The state of being uncorrespondent, or not mutually adapted or agreeable. ''Bp. Gauden.''

'''uncorrespondent†''' (un-kor-e-spon′dent), ''a.'' Not correspondent; not suitable, adapted, or agreeable. ''Bp. Gauden.''

'''uncorrigible†''' (un-kor′i-ji-bl), ''a.'' [< ME. ''uncorrigible''; < ''un-''<sup>1</sup> + ''corrigible''.] Incorrigible. ''Wyclif.''

'''uncorrupt''' (un-ko̤-rupt′), ''a.'' Not corrupt; not depraved; not perverted; incorrupt; pure: as, an ''uncorrupt'' judgment; an ''uncorrupt'' text.

{{smaller block|For the rest, my Lord Clifford was a valiant ''uncorrupt'' gentleman.
{{right|''Evelyn'', Diary, Aug. 18, 1673.}}}}

'''uncorrupted''' (un-ko̤-rup′ted), ''a.'' Not corrupted, in any sense; not debased; not vitiated; not depraved; not decomposed.

{{smaller block|In the chapel belonging to it lies the body of St. Susorius their founder, as yet ''uncorrupted'' though dead many hundreds of yeares.
{{right|''Evelyn'', Diary, Oct. 25, 1644.}}}}

'''uncorruptedness''' (un-ko̤-rup′ted-nes), ''n.'' The state of being uncorrupted. ''Milton'', Areopagitica.

'''uncorruptibility†''' (un-ko̤-rup-ti-bil′i̤-ti), ''n.'' [< ME. ''uncorruptibilitie''; < ''uncorruptible'' + ''-ity'' (see ''-bility'').] Incapability of being corrupted; incorruption.

{{smaller block|In ''vncoruptibilite'' of quyete or pesible and mylde spirit.
{{right|''Wyclif'', 1 Pet. iii. 4.}}}}

'''uncorruptible†''' (un-ko̤-rup′ti-bl), ''a.'' [< ME. ''uncorruptible''; < ''un-''<sup>1</sup> + ''corruptible''.] Incorruptible. Rom. i. 23.

'''uncorruption†''' (un-ko̤-rup′shọn), ''n.'' [< ME. ''uncorrupcioun''; < ''un-''<sup>1</sup> + ''corruption.''] Incorruption.
{{smaller block|Glorie and honour and ''vncoripcioun'' to hem that seken eurlastynge lyf.
{{right|''Wyclif'', Rom. ii. 7.}}}}

'''uncorruptive†''' (un-ko̤-rup′tiv), ''a.'' Incorruptible.
{{smaller block|Those other climes of ''uncorruptive'' joy.
{{right|''Glover'', Leonidas, vii. 413.}}}}

'''uncorruptly''' (un-ko̤-rupt′li), ''adv.'' In an uncorrupt manner; truly; genuinely.
{{smaller block|I shall declare ''uncorruptlye'' the sayings.
{{right|''Brende'', tr. of Quintus Curtius, fol. 198.}}}}

'''uncorruptness''' (un-ko̤-rupt′nes), ''n.'' Integrity; uprightness. Tit. ii. 7.

'''uncorven†''', ''a.'' [ME., < ''un-''<sup>1</sup> + ''corven'', pp. of ''kerven'', carve: see ''carve.''] Uncut; untrimmed.
{{smaller block|''Uncorven'' and ungrobbed lay the vyne.
{{right|''Chaucer'', Former Age, l. 14.}}}}

'''uncostly''' (un-kôst′li), ''a.'' Not costly; not of a high price or value.
{{smaller block|A man’s spirit is naturally careless of baser and ''uncostly'' materials.
{{right|''Jer. Taylor'', Works (ed. 1835), I. 841.}}}}

'''uncounselable, uncounsellable''' (un-koun′sel-a̤-bl), ''a.'' Not to be advised; not consistent with good advice or prudence. ''Clarendon'', Civil Wars.

'''uncounseled, uncounselled''' (un-koun′seld), ''a.'' [< ME. ''uncounceiled''; < ''un-''<sup>1</sup> + ''counseled.''] '''1.''' Not having counsel or advice. ''Burke'', Letter to a Noble Lord.—'''2†.''' Wrongly counseled; led into error.
{{smaller block|''Uncounceiled'' goth ther noon fro me.
{{right|''Rom. of the Rose'', l. 6868.}}}}

'''uncountable''' (un-koun′ta̤-bl), ''a.'' Not capable of being counted; innumerable.
{{smaller block|Those ''uncountable'' bodies set in the firmament.
{{right|''Raleigh'', Hist. World, ii.}}}}

'''uncounted''' (un-koun′ted), ''a.'' Not counted; not numbered; hence, innumerable.
{{smaller block|<poem>The blunt monster with ''uncounted'' heads,
The still-discordant wavering multitude.</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', 2 Hen. IV., Ind.}}
<poem>The twinkling sea’s ''uncounted'' smile.</poem>
{{right|''William Morris'', Earthly Paradise, II. 137.}}}}

'''uncouple''' (un-kup′l), ''v.'' [< ME. ''uncouplen'', ''oncopelen''; < ''un-''<sup>2</sup> + ''couple''.] '''I.''' ''trans.'' To loose, as dogs from their couples, or railway-cars from their couplings; set loose; disjoin.
{{smaller block|<poem>Forth he gothe ther as the hartys hye;
His houndys were ''oncopelyd'' by and by.</poem>
{{right|''Generydes'' (E. E. T. S.), l. 42.}}
<poem>So when our mortal frame shall be disjoined,
The lifeless lump ''uncoupled'' from the mind,
From sense of grief and pain we shall be free.</poem>
{{right|''Dryden'', tr. of Lucretius, iii.}}}}

'''II.''' ''intrans.'' To break loose; exert influence unrestrained.
{{smaller block|<poem>Longe tyme it was er tirannye
Or any vyce dorste on him ''uncouple''.</poem>
{{right|''Chaucer'', Monk’s Tale, l. 512.}}}}

'''uncoupled''' (un-kup′ld), ''a.'' '''1.''' Not coupled; not fastened to a couple or with couplings.
{{smaller block|<poem>Steeds snort, ''uncoupled'' stag-hounds bay,
And merry hunters quit the bower.</poem>
{{right|''Scott'', Cadyow Castle.}}}}

'''2.''' Not wedded; single.
{{smaller block|<poem>''Uncoupled'', cold virginity.</poem>
{{right|''Chamberlayne'', Pharonnida (1659).}}}} '''3.''' In ''her.'', same as ''découplé.''

'''uncourteous''' (un-kėr′tē̤-us), ''a.'' [< ME. ''uncurteis'', ''uncortoise''; < ''un-''<sup>1</sup> + ''courteous.''] Not courteous; uncivil. ''Sir P. Sidney.''='''Syn.''' {{smaller|See ''uncivil.''}}

'''uncourteously''' (un-kėr′tē̤-us-li), ''adv.'' Uncivilly; impolitely. ''Sir T. Elyot'', The Governour, iii. 6.

'''uncourtesy†''', ''n.'' [< ME. ''uncurtesie''; < ''un-''<sup>1</sup> + ''courtesy.''] Lack of courtesy.
{{smaller block|It were to gret ''uncurtesie.'' {{right|''Rom. of the Rose'', l. 3587.}}}}

'''uncourtliness''' (un-kōrt′li-nes), ''n.'' The character of being uncourtly. ''Addison'', Whig-Examiner, No. 5.

'''uncourtly''' (un-kōrt′li), ''a.'' Not courtly. {{smaller|(''a'') Untrained in the manners of a court; hence, not suave, bland, pleasing, flattering, or the like.}}
{{smaller block|<poem>And this event ''uncourtly'' Hero thought
Her inward guilt would in her looks have wrought.</poem>{{right|''Marlowe'', Hero and Leander, iii.}}}}
{{smaller|(''b'') Uncivil; rude; coarse; plain.}}
{{smaller block|It would be ''uncourtly'' to speak in harsher words to the fair. {{right|''Steele'', Spectator, No. 294.}}}}

'''uncous†''' (ung′kus), ''a.'' [< L. ''uncus'', hooked, < ''uncus'', a hook, barb: see ''unce''<sup>2</sup>, ''uncus.''] Hooklike; hooked. ''Sir T. Browne.''

'''uncouth''' (un-köth′), ''a.'' [Also dial. ''unkid'', ''unked'', ''unkard'', Sc. ''unco'' (see ''unco''), < ME. ''uncouth'', ''unkouth'', ''onkouth'', ''uncuth'', ''unkuth'', ''uncothe'', < AS. ''uncūth'' (Icel. ''ūkunnr'' = Goth. ''unkunths''), unknown, unusual, strange; as ''un-''<sup>1</sup> + ''couth.''] '''1.''' Not known. {{smaller|(''a''†) Not common; unusual; rare; hence, elegant; beautiful.}}
{{smaller block|<poem>Ther maystow seen devysing of herneys
So ''uncouth'' and so riche.</poem> {{right|''Chaucer'', Knight’s Tale, l. 1639.}}}}

(''b'') Not commonly known; not familiar; strange; foreign.

{{smaller block|[He] rode be the moste ''vn-couthe'' weyes that thei myght till he com to Newerke. {{right|''Merlin'' (E. E. T. S.), ii. 190.}}}}

<poem>His fall
May be our rise. It is no ''uncouth'' thing
To see fresh buildings from old ruins spring.</poem>{{right|''B. Jonson'', Sejanus, iii. 3.}}

(1†) Strange and suspicious; uncanny; such as to arouse suspicion, dread, fear, or alarm.

{{smaller block|An ''uncouth'' pain torments my grieved soul.{{right|''Marlowe'', Tamburlaine the Great, I., ii. 7.}}}}

{{smaller block|If this ''uncouth'' forest yield anything savage.{{right|''Shak.'', As you Like it, ii. 6. 6.}}}}

{{smaller block|The Judges meet in some ''uncouth'' dark Dungeon.{{right|''Howell'', Letters, I. v. 42.}}}}

(2) Strange and awkward; characterized by awkwardness, clumsiness, or oddity: now the usual meaning: as, ''uncouth'' manners or behavior.

{{smaller block|The terms, the principles, the propositions of it [any human art or science], are all at first sight strange and ''uncouth'', and make no bright impression upon the mind.{{right|''Bp. Atterbury'', Sermons, II. x.}}}}

<poem>Through thee her Merrimacs and Agiochooks
And many a name ''uncouth'' win gracious looks.</poem>{{right|''Lowell'', To Whittier.}}

'''2†.''' Not knowing; ignorant.

{{smaller block|For he taght the ''vn-couthe'' and vn-kunnynge by his prechynge. {{right|''Hampole'', Prose Treatises (E. E. T. S.), p. 25.}}}}

='''Syn. 1''' (''b'') (2). ''Ungainly'', ''Bungling'', etc. See ''awkward''.

'''uncouthly''' (un-köth′li), ''adv.'' [< ME. ''uncouthly'', ''uncuthliȝ'', < AS. ''uncūthlīce'', < ''uncūth'', unknown: see ''uncouth''.] '''1†.''' Rarely; elegantly.

{{smaller block|To graythe [adorn] hir wel and ''uncouthly'' [tr. OF. ''noblement''].{{right|''Rom. of the Rose'', l. 584.}}}}

'''2.''' In an uncouth manner; oddly; strangely; awkwardly; clumsily.<noinclude><references/></noinclude>
